CDMP Fundamentals Exam Study Summary

1CORE DEFINITIONS

Term Definition
Ethics Principles of behavior based on ideas of right and wrong. Often focus on fairness, respect, responsibility, integrity, quality, reliability, transparency, and trust.
Data Handling Ethics Concerned with how to procure, store, manage, interpret, analyze/apply, and dispose of data in ways aligned with ethical principles, including community responsibility.
Privacy by Design Requirement (mandated by GDPR) that privacy protections be built into systems and processes from the start — not added on later.
Data Masking A practice where only appropriate submitted data will unlock processes; operators cannot see the data — only responses given by users unlock further activities.
Data Marking Used to classify data sensitivity (secret, confidential, personal, etc.) and control release to appropriate communities.
Obfuscation / Redaction Making information anonymous or removing sensitive information. May not be sufficient alone if downstream analysis can re-identify individuals.
Data Snooping Exhaustive correlations performed on a dataset that can produce statistically significant-looking results that are actually random — common in financial and medical sectors.
Exam tip

The formal definition of Data Handling Ethics includes the phrase "including community responsibility" — this extends obligations beyond just the organization.

2BUSINESS DRIVERS

  • Ethical data handling is a competitive business advantage (Hasselbalch and Tranberg, 2016)
  • Like W. Edward Deming's view on quality: ethics means "doing it right when no one is looking"
  • Ethical data handling increases trustworthiness of an organization and its data
  • Primary reason for ethical principles: reduce risk that data will be misused by employees, customers, or partners
  • CDMP certification requires data management professionals to subscribe to a formal code of ethics, including an obligation to handle data ethically for the sake of society beyond the employing organization
Exam tip

Know the Deming quote connection — ethics = quality when no one is watching.

3THREE CORE CONCEPTS OF DATA HANDLING ETHICS

  1. Impact on people — Data represents characteristics of individuals; there is an imperative to manage its quality and reliability
  2. Potential for misuse — Misusing data can harm people and organizations; there is an ethical imperative to prevent misuse
  3. Economic value of data — Data has economic value; ethics of data ownership should determine how that value is accessed and by whom

4ETHICAL PRINCIPLES FOR DATA (Belmont Principles — Adapted)

The accepted tenets of bioethics (Belmont Report, US-HSS, 1979) provide the starting point for data ethics:

Principle Meaning in Data Context
Respect for Persons People must be treated in a way that respects their dignity and autonomy. Extra care for people with diminished autonomy. Requires informed, valid consent for data processing.
Beneficence Two elements: (1) Do not harm; (2) maximize possible benefits and minimize possible harms. Is processing unnecessarily invasive? Is there a less risky way to meet the need?
Justice Fair and equitable treatment of people. Are groups treated unequally? Does an algorithm disproportionately benefit or harm a group? Is machine learning reinforcing cultural prejudice?

The US Dept. of Homeland Security's Menlo Report adds a fourth principle:

  • Respect for Law and Public Interest

The European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS, 2015) set four pillars for ethical data ecosystems:

  1. Future-oriented regulation of data processing and respect for privacy
  2. Accountable controllers who determine personal information processing
  3. Privacy-conscious engineering and design of data products/services
  4. Empowered individuals
Exam tip

The Belmont Report was originally for medical research (1979). Know all three principles and that the Menlo Report (DHS) added a fourth.

5PRINCIPLES BEHIND DATA PRIVACY LAW

5.1 OECD Fair Information Processing Standards (1980)

Eight core principles — basis for EU data protection laws:

  1. Limitations on data collection
  2. Data should be of high quality
  3. Data collected for a specific purpose
  4. Limitations on data usage
  5. Security safeguards
  6. Openness and transparency
  7. Individual's right to challenge accuracy of their data
  8. Accountability for organizations
Note

OECD principles were superseded by GDPR principles.

5.2 GDPR Principles (EU, 2016) — Know All 7

GDPR Principle Description
Fairness, Lawfulness, Transparency Personal data shall be processed lawfully, fairly, and in a transparent manner
Purpose Limitation Collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes; not processed incompatibly
Data Minimization Adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary for the purposes
Accuracy Must be accurate and kept up-to-date; inaccurate data must be erased or rectified without delay
Storage Limitation Kept no longer than necessary for the purposes for which processed
Integrity and Confidentiality Appropriate security; protection against unauthorized processing, accidental loss, destruction
Accountability Data Controllers must be able to demonstrate compliance
  • GDPR also mandates Privacy by Design
  • Individual rights include: access, rectification, portability, right to object, right to erasure
  • Consent must be: freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous (affirmative action)

5.3 PIPEDA Principles (Canada) — Know All 9

PIPEDA Principle Key Point
Accountability Organization responsible; must designate an individual accountable for compliance
Identifying Purposes Purposes for collection must be identified at or before time of collection
Consent Must obtain knowledge and consent of individual for collection, use, or disclosure
Limiting Collection, Use, Disclosure, and Retention Limited to what is necessary; retained only as long as necessary
Accuracy Must be accurate, complete, and up-to-date as necessary for purposes
Safeguards Security safeguards appropriate to sensitivity of the information
Openness Policies and practices must be readily available to individuals
Individual Access Individuals can access their data and challenge accuracy
Compliance Challenges Individuals can address compliance challenges to the designated person
  • Canada: Federal Privacy Commissioner has sole responsibility for privacy complaints but fills an ombudsman role — decisions are only recommendations (not legally binding)

5.4 US FTC Privacy Program Criteria — 5 Principles

Principle Description
Notice / Awareness Data collectors must disclose information practices before collecting data
Choice / Consent Consumers must be given options regarding use of their data beyond original purpose
Access / Participation Consumers should be able to view and contest accuracy and completeness of data
Integrity / Security Reasonable steps to assure data is accurate and secure from unauthorized use
Enforcement / Redress Reliable mechanism to impose sanctions for noncompliance

6ONLINE DATA IN AN ETHICAL CONTEXT

Key topics in online data ethics:

  • Ownership of data — rights to control one's personal data vs. data brokers/social media
  • The Right to be Forgotten — to have information about an individual erased from the web; part of data retention practices
  • Identity — right to expect a correct identity and to opt for a private identity
  • Freedom of speech online — expressing opinions vs. bullying, terror inciting, trolling

7RISKS OF UNETHICAL DATA HANDLING (6 Categories)

7.1 Timing

  • Possible to lie through omission or inclusion of data points based on timing
  • Example: Market timing (end-of-day stock trades to artificially raise stock price) — illegal
  • BI staff may be the first to notice such anomalies and have an ethical duty to report them

7.2 Misleading Visualizations

  • Charts/graphs can mislead through:
    • Changing scale (making trend lines look better/worse)
    • Leaving data points out
    • Comparing unrelated facts without context
    • Violating visual conventions (e.g., pie chart percentages not adding to 100)

7.3 Unclear Definitions or Invalid Comparisons

  • Presenting information without context that informs its meaning
  • Data mining snooping — exhaustive correlations produce statistically significant-looking but actually random results
  • The ethical obligation: provide context that informs meaning (clear, unambiguous definitions of populations)

7.4 Bias

  • Bias = an inclination of outlook; in statistics = deviations from expected values
  • Bias can be introduced at: data collection, data selection for analysis, analysis methods, presentation of results

Five types of bias:

  1. Data collection for pre-defined result — collecting data to reach a predetermined conclusion
  2. Biased use of collected data — data collected fairly but used/manipulated to confirm a pre-determined approach
  3. Hunch and search — analyst uses only data that confirms their hunch
  4. Biased sampling methodology — method of selecting the sample introduces bias; use statistical tools to select samples
  5. Context and Culture — biases that are culturally or contextually based
Exam tip

Bias can be introduced at any point in the data lifecycle — collection, selection, analysis, presentation.

7.5 Transforming and Integrating Data

Four ethical risks in data integration:

  1. Limited knowledge of data's origin and lineage — cannot prove data represents what is claimed
  2. Data of poor quality — without measurable quality standards, organization cannot vouch for data
  3. Unreliable Metadata — data may be misunderstood and misused; Metadata should include provenance tags, ownership, and protection requirements
  4. No documentation of data remediation history — data remediation should follow a formal, auditable change control process

7.6 Obfuscation / Redaction of Data

  • Obfuscation alone may not be sufficient if downstream analysis can re-identify individuals
  • Three related practices:
    • Data aggregation — removes PII while retaining analytic value
    • Data marking — classifies data sensitivity; controls release to appropriate communities
    • Data masking — only appropriate responses unlock processes; operators cannot see underlying data

8ESTABLISHING AN ETHICAL DATA CULTURE (4 Steps)

Step 1: Review Current State Data Handling Practices

  • Understand the degree to which practices are connected to ethical and compliance drivers
  • Deliverable: document ethical principles underlying the organization's collection, use, and oversight of data throughout the data lifecycle

Step 2: Identify Principles, Practices, and Risk Factors

  • Purpose: reduce risk that data might be misused and cause harm
  • Must align with legal and regulatory compliance requirements
  • Framework: Principle → Risk → Practice → Control

Example:

  • Principle: People have a right to privacy regarding health data
  • Risk: Wide access could make personal health data public
  • Practice: Only nurses and doctors can access patient health data, only for providing care
  • Control: Annual review of all users of systems containing patient health information

Step 3: Create an Ethical Data Handling Strategy and Roadmap

Components:

  • Values statements — describe what the organization believes in (truth, fairness, justice)
  • Ethical data handling principles — how the organization approaches challenges (e.g., respecting right to privacy)
  • Compliance framework — factors driving organizational obligations (geographic and sector concerns)
  • Risk assessments — identify likelihood and implications of specific problems
  • Training and communications — employees must sign off that they are familiar with the code of ethics; requires annual ethics statement affirmation
  • Roadmap — timeline with management-approved activities
  • Approach to auditing and monitoring — reinforce ethical ideas through monitoring

Step 4: Adopt a Socially Responsible Ethical Risk Model

  • Data professionals in BI, analytics, and Data Science have access to data about:
    • Who people are (demographic, racial, ethnic, religious characteristics)
    • What people do (political, social, potentially criminal activities)
    • Where people live, financial data, purchasing, communications
    • How people are treated (scoring, preference tracking, privileges)
  • This data can counteract the ethical principles of Respect for Persons, Beneficence, and Justice
  • Organizations have a social responsibility not to do harm with their data
  • Automated monitoring alone is not sufficient — people/analysts must reflect on possible bias

Four areas of ethical consideration in analytics projects:

  1. How populations are selected for study
  2. How data will be captured
  3. What activities analytics will focus on
  4. How the results will be made accessible

9DATA ETHICS AND GOVERNANCE

  • Oversight for appropriate data handling falls under Data Governance and legal counsel
  • Together they must: keep up-to-date on legal changes AND reduce risk of ethical impropriety
  • Data Governance responsibilities:
    • Set standards and policies for data handling practices
    • Provide oversight
    • Review plans/decisions proposed by BI, analytics, and Data Science studies
    • Ensure employees are aware of their obligations
  • Employees must expect: fair handling, protection from reporting breaches, non-interference in personal lives
  • CDMP certification requires subscribing to a formal code of ethics — obligation to handle data ethically for society beyond the employing organization
Exam tip

Data Governance has a specific oversight requirement to review plans and decisions proposed by BI, analytics, and Data Science studies.

10CONTEXT DIAGRAM SNAPSHOT

Element Detail
Definition How to procure, store, manage, interpret, analyze/apply, and dispose of data in ways aligned with ethical principles, including community responsibility
Goals (1) Define ethical handling; (2) Educate staff on risks; (3) Change/instill preferred culture and behaviors; (4) Monitor regulatory environment, measure, monitor, and adjust
Activities (P) Review Practices; (P) Identify Principles & Risk Factors; Create Strategy; (D) Address Practice Gaps; (D) Communicate & Educate; (C) Monitor & Maintain Alignment
Key Deliverables Current Practices & Gaps, Ethical Data Handling Strategy, Communication Plan, Ethics Training Program, Ethical Corporate Statements, Updated Policies, Ethical Data Handling Reporting
Metrics Number of Employees Trained, Compliance/Non-compliance Incidents, Corporate Executive Involvement
Techniques Communication Plan Checklists, Annual Ethics Statement Affirmations

11HIGH-PROBABILITY EXAM QUESTIONS

Q1. What is the formal DMBOK definition of Data Handling Ethics?

Concerned with how to procure, store, manage, interpret, analyze/apply, and dispose of data in ways aligned with ethical principles, including community responsibility.

Q2. What are the three core concepts at the center of data handling ethics?

(1) Impact on people, (2) Potential for misuse, (3) Economic value of data

Q3. The Belmont Principles were originally developed for what field?

Medical/biomedical research (US-HSS, 1979). Adapted for Information Management.

Q4. Name the three Belmont Principles and the fourth added by the Menlo Report.

Belmont: Respect for Persons, Beneficence, Justice. Menlo adds: Respect for Law and Public Interest.

Q5. What does "Beneficence" mean in the context of data ethics?

Two elements: (1) Do not harm; (2) maximize possible benefits and minimize possible harms.

Q6. What are the 7 GDPR principles?

Fairness/Lawfulness/Transparency, Purpose Limitation, Data Minimization, Accuracy, Storage Limitation, Integrity and Confidentiality, Accountability.

Q7. What does GDPR mandate regarding privacy in system design?

Privacy by Design — privacy must be built into systems and processes from the start.

Q8. What is the GDPR requirement for consent?

Must be an affirmative action that is freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous.

Q9. Under PIPEDA, who handles privacy complaints in Canada?

The Federal Privacy Commissioner — but fills an ombudsman role; decisions are only recommendations (not legally binding).

Q10. What is the OECD relationship to GDPR?

OECD's 8 Fair Information Processing Standards (1980) were the basis for EU data protection laws but have since been superseded by GDPR principles.

Q11. What is "data snooping"?

Exhaustive correlations on a data set that produce statistically significant-looking results that are actually random — common in financial and medical sectors.

Q12. At what points in the data lifecycle can bias be introduced?

At data collection, selection for analysis, analysis methods, and presentation of results — at any point in the lifecycle.

Q13. What is the difference between data masking and data marking?

Data marking classifies data sensitivity (secret, confidential, personal) to control release. Data masking allows only appropriate responses to unlock processes — operators cannot see the underlying data.

Q14. Why is obfuscation alone not sufficient to protect data?

Because downstream analysis or combination with other datasets can re-identify individuals, even from anonymized data. Particularly a risk in large data sets and data lakes.

Q15. What is the PIPEDA principle about identifying purposes?

Purposes for collection must be identified at or before the time information is collected.

Q16. What does the CDMP code of ethics require regarding data?

CDMP holders must handle data ethically for the sake of society beyond the organization that employs them.

Q17. What four areas should analytics projects account for in an ethical risk model?

(1) How populations are selected; (2) How data is captured; (3) What analytics will focus on; (4) How results are made accessible.

Q18. What is the role of Data Governance in data ethics?

Set standards and policies, provide oversight of data handling practices, and specifically review plans and decisions proposed by BI, analytics, and Data Science studies.

Q19. Is automated monitoring sufficient protection from unethical data practices?

No — people (analysts themselves) need to reflect on possible bias. Cultural norms influence corporate behavior.

Q20. What is the W. Edward Deming quote used in the context of data ethics?

"Doing it right when no one is looking."
